newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish floods strike major city Wroclaw's suburbs.
newsitem.headline: Polish floods strike major city Wroclaw's suburbs.

text.p: A swell of high water raging north along the Odra River from Poland's heavily flooded south reached the major city of Wroclaw on Saturday and within minutes swamped some of its southern suburbs.

A local government spokesman said authorities were deciding to breach flood walls further south of the city to free some water into the countryside and save the historic centre from the horror endured by some 50 Polish towns and 300 villages.

The floods caused by heavy rains throughout much of this week have already claimed at least 24 lives and caused tens of thousands of people to be evacuated, leaving some villages eerily deserted and resembling tragic parodies of Venice.

"A decision is being taken to breach barriers to divert water eastward into the Widawa valley...so as to prevent a thorough flooding of the city," spokesman Ludwik Ryng told Reuters by telephone. "Otherwise there is a real danger."
In communities just upstream of Wroclaw, including Siechnice, water surged over defences and reached the first storey of buildings.
Alarmed residents, shocked by the speed of the waters' advance, scurried to upper floors and rooftops to await rescue by emergency services and troops in boats and helicopters.

Reuter photographer Pawel Kopczynski, on the scene, said waters in central Wroclaw were almost touching bridges and teams of workers were frantically laying sandbags to protect the low-lying island with a church and historic mill.
Precious old books and archives were being hastily removed from a university library on the Tumski island of the city, known in German as Breslau.
In the suburban community of Korzanow the fast, filthy waters were lapping at the base of 10 storey apartment blocs.
"The water took only half an hour to sweep in and now in some places it is one or even two metres deep," Kopczynski reported.

The city of Opole, further south, on Friday gave a terrifying foretaste of the fate that could await the 650,000 people of Wroclaw, when the waters coursed right into the centre and people took refuge in high-rise buildings.

Many citizens and nearby villagers had disregarded warnings to leave their homes in advance, for fear of looters or from a desire to stay with everything they held dear, and had to be coaxed by rescuers into boats after the floods arrived.

"Above all, the old people are terrified climbing into the precarious little boats. Some people were angry, they said not enough was being done for them, many didn't want to leave their houses until the last moment," Kopczynski reported.
By Friday there were at least 365,000 hectares, or about 3,500 sq km (2,170 sq miles), of Poland under water owing to the floods, which have also ravaged the Czech Republic.
Prime Minister Wlodzimierz assured Poles in a televised address late on Friday that helping victims of the flood would be the government's priority.
"We are now working on next year's budget draft and extra means needed for liquidating effects of the flood will be taken into account," he said.
He added the government was considering borrowing money abroad to help victims of the flood and was in talks with the World Bank on a big loan for the purpose.

The floods could hurt the main ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) party of former communists, facing a close fight against rightists grouped round the Solidarity trade union in parliamentary elections on September 21.
Opposition critics accuse the government of doing too little, too late -- charges the prime minister rejects.
